cards.explanation: The answer is True. The text says Milcah is the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. That's the same Haran who died in Ur, and he was Nahor's brother. So Nahor's wife comes from his own brother's household. Genesis keeps its family records tight, friends.

The answer is that she has no children. The text says, “But Sarai was barren; she had no children.” Notice how short that is after all those long lists of sons and daughters, friends. It reads like the writer set down his pen and let the quiet sit there. I think that quiet is the whole point.

The answer is False. Terah does not leave Lot behind. The text says Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai. So Lot goes with them when they set out from Ur. His father Haran died back in Ur, and Lot is still part of the family caravan, friends.

The answer is Haran. The text says that when they arrived in Haran, they settled there. It's the same name as Terah's son Haran, who died in Ur, so keep them straight, bakers: one is a man and one is a place. They set out for Canaan, and this is where they stop instead.

The answer is that he dies there. Terah lives 205 years, and he dies in Haran. The family set out for Canaan, but Terah's story ends there in Haran. The writer doesn't dress it up, and neither will I, friends. Sometimes the plain truth is the whole lesson.

The answer is to a land God will show him. God says, “…go to the land I will show you.” In His words to Abram, the place isn't named, only the promise that He will show him. That takes real trust, friends. I'd have asked for directions twice and then packed extra cookie boxes.

The answer is a great nation. God says, “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you…” A nation is a whole lot of people, friends. That's like holding one lonely cookie and being told it will fill a stadium. Now that's a promise with some size to it.

The answer is True. God says, “I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.” Notice the “so that,” friends. The name is tied to being a blessing. That's how God puts it, and the very next thing He says is that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram.

The answer is to all the families of the earth. God says, “…all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” That's not just one neighborhood, friends. It's every family on earth. For a man who hasn't even found the land yet, that's a promise bigger than the whole map.

The answer is True. The text says, “So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him…” He has the promises but not the address, and he goes anyway, friends. The text also tells us he was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

The answer is True. The text says Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all their possessions and people, and set out for the land of Canaan. Then it says, “When they came to the land of Canaan…” Terah's trip stopped in Haran, friends, but this one gets all the way there.

The answer is False, and the land is not empty. Abram travels through the land as far as the Oak of Moreh at Shechem (Genesis 12:6). Then the text says, “And at that time the Canaanites were in the land.” So the land has people in it already, bakers. Abram shows up as the new face in town, and I bet he didn't know where the good parking was.

The answer is Abram's offspring. The LORD says, “I will give this land to your offspring.” Offspring means Abram's descendants, the family that's still to come. Think about it, friends. Sarai has no children yet, and God is already talking about a whole inheritance.

The answer is an altar. The text says, “So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.” He builds it right where the LORD appeared, friends. The promise was spoken, and an altar went up.

The answer is True. The text says Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent. Then, “There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.” That makes a second altar in the land, friends, after the one where the LORD appeared to him.
